opus-5.5.text:
I should say up front that I'm an American looking in from the outside. Most of what I know about China's AI ecosystem comes from reading the papers, using the open models, and talking with researchers there. So take this as one observer's impression.

The biggest difference I see is in how each side frames the technology. In the US, especially in the Bay Area, the conversation is very abstract and existential. People talk about AGI timelines, superintelligence, whether we're building something that replaces us. There's a lot of anxiety mixed with a lot of hype. The public reaction is also quite skeptical. Polling consistently shows Americans are more worried than excited about AI, and there's real backlash around jobs, copyright, and data centers.

In China, what I observe is much more pragmatic. AI gets talked about as infrastructure, like electricity or the internet, a tool you deploy into manufacturing, logistics, consumer apps. There's still a race narrative, but it's more about catching up and building industrial capacity than about some singular moment of AGI. Public sentiment also seems more optimistic. People there have lived through enormous technological change in a short time, and for many of them it's been tied to rising living standards. That makes the default reaction less fearful.

You can see this in how the labs behave. Chinese labs like DeepSeek, Qwen, and Moonshot have leaned hard into open-weight releases, partly from strategy, partly from necessity under compute constraints, and partly from an engineering culture that wants to show results and get adoption. American frontier labs have mostly gone closed. They justify that with safety arguments and commercial ones. That divergence is one of the most important things happening in AI right now, and it's why I've been vocal that the US needs a stronger open-model ecosystem of its own.

One caveat: both countries are much less monolithic than these generalizations suggest. There are safety-minded researchers in China and plenty of "just ship it" pragmatists in the US. But the center of gravity in each conversation really does feel different.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Chinese developers’ unease about AI changing software work or whether that unease has become a collective judgment.

r002.rationale: It says people in China have experienced enormous technological change tied to rising living standards, which makes them less fearful of AI—a clear equivalent of treating it as another familiar wave of change.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute greater American resistance to longer intervals between previous waves of technological change.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I should say up front that I'm an American researcher looking at this from the outside, so I want to be careful about overclaiming on the Chinese side. But I've spent a lot of time tracking the open model ecosystem, and the contrast is pretty striking.

In the US, the dominant emotional register around AI right now is anxiety. You see it in the discourse about jobs, in the safety debates, in how people talk about open weights as this potentially dangerous thing that needs to be controlled. There's a lot of hedging, a lot of "we need to slow down and think about this." And the big labs are mostly closed, so the public conversation happens at the level of narratives and fears rather than people actually touching the technology.

What I see coming out of China, at least through the lens of the labs and the developers, is a much more pragmatic, almost matter-of-fact attitude. Technology changes things, you adapt, you build. DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, all these groups are shipping open models at a pace that frankly embarrassed a lot of American companies. And culturally there seems to be less hand-wringing about whether this should exist and more energy going into making it work and getting it into people's hands.

Part of that is history. China has lived through enormous, fast technological transitions in living memory. The mobile payments shift, the whole super-app era. People have seen their daily lives reorganized by technology within a decade, and it mostly went fine for them, or at least it became normal. In the US, the last really transformative consumer tech wave was maybe smartphones and social media, and the retrospective on social media is quite negative. So the prior that a lot of Americans bring to AI is "the last time this happened, it kind of hurt us."

There's also a policy dimension. Chinese leadership has been very explicit that AI is a strategic priority and that open models are a way to gain influence and adoption globally. That gives the labs a clear direction. In the US, the government posture is much more fragmented, swinging between "race China" and "regulate everything," and companies are navigating that ambiguity.

The caveat I'd add is that I think I'm mostly seeing the builder class on both sides. I don't have great visibility into how an ordinary person in a Chinese city feels about losing a job to a model. My guess is the human reactions are more similar than the institutional ones. But at the level of how the ecosystems are behaving, China is treating this as an opportunity to grab and the US is still debating whether it's an opportunity or a threat. And honestly, that gap in attitude explains a lot about why the open model leaderboard looks the way it does right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes Chinese builders as pragmatic and says ordinary people’s reactions may be more similar, but it does not state that developers’ unease about AI changing software work has not become a collective view that AI is bad and will destroy society.

r002.rationale: It says China has experienced rapid technological transitions in living memory, that daily life was reorganized within a decade, and that these changes became normal—presenting AI as another familiar wave of change.

r003.rationale: It says Americans view the last major consumer technology wave negatively, but does not attribute greater resistance to longer intervals between previous waves of change.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about treating either country as having one reaction. But one useful way to think about it is whether people see AI primarily as an opportunity to build or as a disruption they need to manage.

In the United States, those attitudes coexist. You have enormous optimism and investment in Silicon Valley, alongside anxiety about jobs, safety, and who will capture the benefits. And those can be the same person: someone can love using an AI tool and still worry about what it means for their career.

My impression is that the Chinese conversation can put more emphasis on technological progress as a source of economic opportunity and national competitiveness. But I wouldn’t jump from that to saying Chinese people are uniformly optimistic or Americans are pessimistic. Which people you’re listening to matters enormously—engineers, workers, policymakers, or company leaders.

So I’d frame the difference less as enthusiasm versus fear, and more as expectations: what do people think this technology will do for them, and do they trust the institutions deploying it to make that change beneficial?

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss Chinese developers’ unease about AI’s effects on software work or whether they see AI as socially destructive.

r002.rationale: It mentions Chinese emphasis on progress and opportunity, but does not connect that outlook to repeated rapid technological or economic changes.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute American resistance to longer intervals between prior waves of technological change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful way to understand it is to ask whether people see technological change as an opportunity or as a threat to something they already have. In China, rapid technological development can be associated with rising living standards and national progress. In the U.S., you hear a lot more concern about what AI might disrupt—jobs, creative work, or institutions people value.

But I’d be careful about making that a clean national distinction. An American AI founder and an American worker worried about automation may have very different reactions, and the same kinds of differences exist in China. The question is partly about who expects to benefit, who expects to bear the costs, and whether they trust the institutions managing the transition.

So I wouldn’t say one society understands AI better. I’d say people are approaching the same technology with different experiences of change and different expectations about where it will take them.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss Chinese developers’ unease or whether it has become a collective judgment that AI will harm society.

r002.rationale: It links China’s rapid technological development with progress, but does not say repeated waves of change make AI feel familiar.

r003.rationale: It describes greater U.S. concern about disruption, but does not attribute that to longer intervals between earlier waves of change.
